     SOME RESULTS AND CONJECTURES RELATED TO FRANKL’S UNION
                       CLOSED CONJECTURE

                                   REIN VAN DER HOUT, KEES ROOS∗

     Department of Mathematics, Delft University of Technology, Mekelweg 2, 2628 CD Delft, Netherlands

Abstract. A union-closed family F is a finite collection of distinct subsets of a finite set such that the
union of two subsets in F belongs to F . Péter Frankl conjectured in 1979 that, for any such family,
there exists an element that belongs to at least half of its sets. This conjecture is still unsolved. In this
paper, we present some results and conjectures related to Frankl’s conjecture. The new conjectures are
based on evidence provided by some experimental results.
Keywords. Conjecture of Frankl; Optimization model; Power set; Union-closed sets.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. 05D05.

                                           1. I NTRODUCTION
  In this paper, we use the following notations:
                            X     :   a finite set;
                            2X    :   the family of all subsets of X;
                            F     :   a family of distinct subsets of X;
                            Fx    :   the subsets in F that contain x ∈ X.
A family F is called union-closed if S ∪ T ∈ F for any two subsets S ∈ F and T ∈ F . We then
say that F is a UC-family. In this paper, we deal with the so-called union-closed conjecture
(UCC):
Conjecture 1.1. If F is a UC-family, then at least one element x ∈ X belongs to at least half of
the sets in F .
   Without loss of generality, we assume that 0/ ∈ F , where 0/ denotes the empty set. For a
simple proof, we refer to [6, Lemma 1]. When F contains only the empty set, the conjecture
fails because then |Fx | = 0 for every x and |F | = 1. This case will always be excluded below.
   The UCC was mentioned first in [3], by Péter Frankl, where he wrote 1979 as its year of
origin. Since then, the conjecture became also known as the Frankl conjecture. Many solution
attempts yielded several partial results; see [2, 6, 9, 10] for some early results from the previous
century. Below we mention some of these results that are relevant for the current paper. For a

quite complete historical survey up to 2015, we refer to [1]. But, after more than 45 years, the
conjecture is still open.
Remark 1.1. It may be noted that, in [3], Frankl deals with intersection-closed (or IC-) families
G , for which S ∩ T ∈ G holds for any two subsets S ∈ G and T ∈ G . There he conjectured the
existence of an element x ∈ X that belongs to at most half of the subsets in G . By taking for
G the complements of the sets in a UC family F the two conjectures turn out to be equivalent.
This is a consequence of the well-known theorem of De Morgan: the complement of the union
of two sets is equal to the intersection of their complements.
   Recently, the interest in the UCC was renewed due to a paper of Gilmer [4]. He showed the
existence of an element x ∈ X belonging to at least 1% of the subsets in F . This was considered
to be a breakthrough. It has led to some improvements up to slightly more than 38% instead of
1% [5, 11, 12]. Hopefully the current paper brings us closer to a clear yes or no answer to the
UCC.
   We call an element x ∈ X as in the conjecture a Frankl element. With Fx as defined above,
the UCC can be stated as follows:
                         F is UC ⇒ ∃x ∈ X such that |Fx | ≥ 21 |F | ,
where we use |.| to denote the cardinality of a set or family.
   In this paper, the focus is on tight UC-families. We call a UC-family F tight if every element
of X belongs to at most half of the sets in F . More precisely, a UC-family F is tight if and
only if
                                       |Fx | ≤ 12 |F | , ∀x ∈ X.
The relevance of this focus may be clear: if F is not tight, then the existence of a Frankl element
is obvious, because then |Fx | > 12 |F | for at least one x ∈ X. So, for proving the UCC, it suffices
to consider tight UC-families. For such families, the UCC requires only that |Fx | = 12 |F | for
some x ∈ X. One surprising result of our research is that there is strong evidence that in the tight
case |Fx | = 12 |F | holds for every x ∈ X. One may easily understand that this certainly holds if
F is the power set of X, i.e., if F = 2X for some finite set X.

                                       2. A N O LD R ESULT
  For future use, we present in this section one of the oldest results in [9, Theorem 1].
Theorem 2.1. If the UCC holds for all UC-families F with |F | odd, then it also holds for all
UC-families F with |F | even.
Proof. Suppose that F is a UC-family with |F | = 2k for some k > 1. Let U ∈ F be such that
U 6= 0/ and |U| minimal. Then U is not the union of two distinct nonempty sets in F . Therefore,
the family G that arises from F by removing U will be a UC-family of size 2k − 1. Since |G |
is odd, the assumption in the theorem implies that G satisfies the UCC. So, |Gx | ≥ 12 |G | = k − 21
for some x. Hence |Gx | ≥ k = 12 |F |. Since G ⊆ F implies |Gx | ≤ |Fx | for every x, we may
conclude that F satisfies the UCC.                                                               
   A natural question is whether the converse also holds: if the UCC holds whenever |F | is
even does it then also always hold when |F | is odd? If this were true, then a simple induction
argument would yield that the UCC holds for every UC-family, since it obviously holds if
|F | = 2. But, as pointed out in [1], naive induction does not succeed in the UCC case.

                                 3. T WO OTHER O LD R ESULTS
  In this section, we present a new proof of two other old results, namely that if a UC-family
F contains a singleton (or 1-set) {x}, then x is a Frankl element, and if F contains a 2-set
{x, y}, then either x or y is a Frankl element. We first deal with the case where F contains a
2-set. After this the case where F contains a 1-set easily follows. The proof below uses only
two elementary facts, namely the law of De Morgan and
                            |S ∪ T | = |S| + |T | − |S ∩ T |, ∀S, T ⊆ X.                       (3.1)
Theorem 3.1. Let F be UC and {x, y} ∈ F . Then either |Fx | ≥ 21 |F | or Fy ≥ 12 |F |.
Proof. Let Fx 0 denote the complement of Fx in F and similarly for y. We define the mapping
ϕ : Fx 0 ∩ Fy 0 → Fx ∩ Fy as follows:
                       ϕ(U) = U ∪ {x, y} ∈ Fx ∩ Fy ,       ∀U ∈ Fx 0 ∩ Fy 0 .
One easily verifies that ϕ is injective. Hence
                                      Fx ∩ Fy ≥ |Fx 0 ∩ Fy 0 |.                                (3.2)
According to De Morgan’s theorem, the complement of Fx 0 ∩ Fy 0 in F is Fx ∪ Fy . Hence, by
adding the cardinality of Fx ∪ Fy to both sides of (3.2), we obtain
                                  |Fx ∩ Fy | + |Fx ∪ Fy | ≥ |F |.
Due to (3.1), the sum at the left equals |Fx | + |Fy |. Hence |Fx | + |Fy | ≥ |F |, which implies
the lemma.                                                                                     
Corollary 3.1. If a UC-family F contains a singleton, then it satisfies the UCC.
Proof. Take y = x in Lemma 3.1.                                                             
   We conclude from the above results that if a UC-family contains a subset S which is a 1-set
or a 2-set, then S contains a Frankl element.

                                 4. S OME R ESULTS ON 3- SETS
   Probably Sarvate and Renaud were the first to prove the results in the previous section, at least
for 2-sets [9, Theorem 2]. In a subsequent paper, they showed that there is no such result for
3-sets [10]. They demonstrated this by presenting a UC family with 27 subsets of a set X with
|X| = 9 whose smallest set is a 3-set which does not contain a Frankl element. In their example,
the family does not contain the empty set. Later on, Poonen gave a different example in [6,
page 267] with 28 subsets of the same set X. We found a smaller example F , given in Figure 1
by its matrix representation AF . This 19 × 7 matrix is the so-called binary representation of a
family F consisting of 19 subsets of a set with 7 elements. Its rows are the (binary) incidence
vectors of the subsets in F . So the first row represents the empty set, the second row the 3-set
Y = {1, 2, 3} and the third row the set {4, 5, 7} and so on. We leave it to the reader to verify that
F is a UC family. The column sums of AF are respectively 9, 9, 9, 14, 14, 14, and 17. Since

                              6. F OUR R ELATED C ONJECTURES
   We made clear in Section 1 that it suffices to prove the UCC for the tight case.
   As we saw that, in Table 2, it may happen that Fy = Fx for x, y ∈ X. We then say that
x and y are equivalent, denoting this as x ' y. Indeed, ' is an equivalence relation in the
formal sense. Following Poonen [6], its equivalence classes are called blocks. If x and y are
equivalent elements then one of these elements can be neglected, because this hurts neither the
UC-property nor the UCC. After doing this the blocks becomes singletons. A family will be
called clean if its blocks are singletons and there are no ’idle’ elements, i.e., elements x with
|Fx | = 0. Our ultimate goal is to show that if a tight UC-family is clean then it is a power set.
   We use U 0 to denote the complement of any subset U of X. If F is a clean UC-family, it
contains the set X. As mentioned before, we assume that F also contains its complement X 0 ,
which is the empty set. Hence, we always have |F | ≥ 2 and |Fx | ≥ 1 for every x ∈ X.
   We proceed with a simple lemma.
Lemma 6.1. If F is closed under taking complements, then |Fx | = 21 |F | for each x ∈ X.
Proof. For each subset U in F and for each element x in X we have either x ∈ U or x ∈ U 0 .
Since U 0 also belongs to F , x belongs to exactly half of the number of sets in F . This implies
the lemma.                                                                                     
  Taking into account our assumption that F is clean we have the following four conjectures.
Conjecture 6.1. If F is UC and tight, then F = 2X .
Conjecture 6.2. If F is UC and tight, then U ∈ F implies U 0 ∈ F .
Conjecture 6.3. If F is UC and tight, then |Fx | = 12 |F | for every x ∈ X.
Conjecture 6.4. If F is UC and tight, then |F | is even.
Proposition 6.1. One has the following implications:
     Conjecture 6.1 ⇒ Conjecture 6.2 ⇒ Conjecture 6.3 ⇒ Conjecture 6.4 ⇒ UCC.
Proof. Since the power set 2X of X is closed under taking complements the implication from
Conjecture 6.1 to Conjecture 6.2 is trivial. The implication from Conjecture 6.2 to Conjecture
6.3 is an immediate consequence of Lemma 6.1. Furthermore, if Conjecture 6.3 holds then
Conjecture 6.4 also holds, because |F | ≥ 2 and |F |/2 is integral. Finally we deal with the
implication from Conjecture 6.4 to the UCC. Let F be a UC-family with |F | odd. Then
Conjecture 6.4 implies that F is not tight. But this means that F satisfies the UCC. This
proves that all odd UC-families satisfy the UCC. By Theorem 2.1 this implies that also all UC-
families with |F | even satisfy the UUC. Hence, Conjecture 6.4 implies that the UCC always
holds. This completes the proof.                                                             
   We conclude this section by proving the inverse implications of two of the four implications
in Proposition 6.1.
                                   FRANKL’S UNION CLOSED CONJECTURE                                           17

Proposition 6.2. The UCC implies Conjecture 6.4.
Proof. Assuming the UCC, we let F be a tight UC-family. The UC property implies that
|Fx | ≥ 12 |F | for some x ∈ X. The tightness of F implies |Fx | ≤ 12 |F |. Hence we obtain
|Fx | = 12 |F |. Since |Fx | is integral, it follows that |F | is even.                       
   Apparently, due to the last two propositions we may conclude that Conjecture 6.4 is equiva-
lent with the UCC. We do not yet know if this also holds true for the conjectures 6.1 to 6.3.
   For the proof of the second inverse implication we need one more lemma.
Lemma 6.2. If F is UC and closed under taking complements, then F is closed under taking
intersections.
Proof. Let F be UC and closed under taking complements and U,V ∈ F . Then also U 0 ,V 0 ∈ F
and due to the UC-property also U 0 ∪V 0 ∈ F . Using De Morgan’s law, we may now write
                                                    0
                                  U ∩V = U 0 ∪V 0 ∈ F .
This proves the lemma.                                                                                       

and tight, and therefore by Conjecture 6.2 also closed under taking complements. By Lemma
6.2, this implies that F is IC. Now let x ∈ X and

                                             7. C ONCLUSION
  It is almost incomprehensible that a basic problem as Frankl’s conjecture has remained un-
solved for so long. Every mathematician should feel challenged by this fundamental problem.
As should be clear, this short note leaves the conjecture open. But hopefully it brings us some-
how closer to the solution.
  On the other hand, it may well be one of those problems that are beyond the capacity of the
human mind, just to remind us that there are things we will never understand [7].
